utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-84bis-T, The Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj, Idriz Balaj and Lahi Brahimaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we have the appearances for today, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Your Honours. Paul Rogers, and Ms. Daniela Kravetz for the Prosecution together with our case manager, Line Pedersen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rogers. And for Mr. Haradinaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Ben Emmerson, together with Rod Dixon, Annie O'Reilly, Andrew Strong and we're joined today by Daniel Gad el rab.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And for Mr. Balaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Gregor Guy-Smith, Colleen Rohan, Chad Mair on behalf of Mr. Balaj. Mr. Zyberi is no longer with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Guy-Smith. And for Mr. Brahimaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Richard Harvey, assisted by Mr. Paul Troop and Mr. Luke Boenisch. I should have notified Your Honours, just as Mr. Zyberi is no longer available to assist Mr. Guy-Smith, Ms. Jasini is no longer available to assist me, which means that both of our teams have lost their Albanian-speaking members, but I just pass that on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harvey. May we pleas move into closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, before we do move into closed session, I think we probably already have.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: There's a matter I'd like to raise in open session, if I may, before the witness is brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Okay. Wait a minute with the blinds there, sir. Madam Registrar, can you take us back into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, yesterday, I caused a letter to be sent to Prosecution counsel, in light of matters that the court was discussing yesterday. There are several matters that arise as a result of that, and I think Your Honours would be assisted if I could hand to you copies of correspondence and documents received from the Prosecution as a result. There are three copies here for Your Honours; one for the Registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you tendering them as exhibits [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: No. I'm providing them for your assistance because I wish to take you through them and indicate to you the position we have reached today, which I think is one that is profoundly disturbing and on which I will be seeking your guidance in due course. But I think you're going to need to follow these with me. I just want to be as helpful to everybody as possible, so that you can see what this is about. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: As far as I'm concerned these documents arrived 4 minutes before I walked into court. I'm not sure when the Prosecution served them but I think it was shortly before 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: 1.52 is the time of the e-mail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honours will see, first of all, the first sheet you have is in fact the reply. I'd like if you would be kind enough to turn to page two which was my letter sent by my Case Manager yesterday at 6.12 p.m., while I was on my feet, and which I wrote to Mr. Rogers in the following terms: [As read] "In the light of the questions you asked of the witness in private session," and I give the transcript reference there, "it is evident that you are in possession of further information concerning this witness's application for asylum refugee status. I would therefore be grateful if you would urgently, i.e., by close of business today," that is to say yesterday, "disclose all document and information in your possession concerning the witness's application for asylum refugee status in order that I may consider the material and use it, if appropriate, in cross-examination. This includes, but should not be considered limited to: 1, any correspondence between the OTP and any other party such as the country's authorities, lawyers or intermediaries acting on behalf of the witness; 2, documentation evidencing the progress of and outcome of the witness's application for asylum and/or refugee status; 3, subsequent proceedings brought by the authorities to deport or remove the witness from the country; 4, submissions or representations made by the OTP to the country's authorities to enable the witness to return to that country if he were to leave that country in order to testify, having been refused permission to remain in that country. "I would be grateful if you would consider this request and of the utmost urgency." You will see then if you turn back to page 1, Your Honours, the response, and you will see that it is timed at 1.52 p.m. today: [As read] "Dear counsel: I write in response to Mr. Harvey's disclosure request, in which he asks for urgent disclosure of all documents," et cetera. And then taken in this order: [As read] "In relation to item 3" -- and Your Honours may just want to have -- cast your eyes back to page 2 again. "In relation to item 3, the Prosecution has no information in this regard. In relation to item 4," that's submissions or representations made by the OTP, "no such submissions or representations have been made by the OTP. Travel arrangements for witnesses are handled by VWS. In relation to item, the OTP received from the witness's attorney, on Tuesday, the 30th of August, and as we all know, that's the day before yesterday, a copy of the most recent decision relating to the witness's application. We contacted the attorney yesterday afternoon to inquire whether this decision was subject to any privilege. He has informed that this should be treated confidentially and only referred to in private session. Especially as the witness has not seen or been made privy to it himself. This decision is attached. The only other information about the status of the witness's application was contained in the attorney's original e-mail of 5 November 2010, in which he informed the OTP that the witness had recently been denied political asylum and that his case was pending before the (redacted). "Finally, in relations to item 1, that's a request for any correspondence between the OTP and any other party such as the country's authorities, lawyers, or intermediaries acting on behalf of the witness, we are looking into this request and will revert to you in due course." Accompanying that e-mail were the items that Your Honours will find and which, since it is asked by the witness's attorney in the country that these matters should be treated confidentially, I'm not going to read them. But save to say, the first item that Your Honours have, I believe is an e-mail message from Mr. Roel Versonnen, the investigator of the Prosecution, dated the 2nd of February, 2011, to the witness, in response to a message from that witness which appears to be dated that same day. And Your Honours will see the content of that, in my submission, eminently disclosable document, which was disclosed to me at 1.52 p.m. today. And I give Your Honours a moment to read what the witness wrote to Mr. Versonnen. And finally, Your Honours, if you have finished with that, we have the decision of the (redacted) -- ooh. I'm sorry. Can we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Madam Registrar, could be please redact that reference to that country in page 5, line 23. Are you done, Madam Registrar? May we then move into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: My apologies to everyone. We'll see the decision that was dated the 26th of August, the last month. And you'll see in material part, and I --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. If this is to be referred to, it must be referred to in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Yes, I accept that. May this be -- may we go into private session for this part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, you will see after a number of procedural issues are dealt with, first of all, it appears that the -- on the 16th of June, 2010, an immigration judge denied the witness's applications for asylum, withholding of removal and protection under the UN convention against torture, finding that the applicant established past persecution, however, the immigration judge also found that the (redacted) met its burden with respect to both a fundamental change in circumstances, such that the applicant no longer had a well-founded fear of persecution in Kosovo and the availability of internal relocation. There was then a further decision on -- actually, it would appear an earlier decision on March 10th -- no, I'm sorry. Further decision March 10th, 2011, denying the applicant's motion to remand and dismissing the appeals. However, it appears from the next paragraph that the letter that Your Honours saw yesterday from Mr. Rogers was submitted to the -- to the court for -- as part of an application for review. And in that, it was noted that the applicant provided a voluntary witness statement, in relation to this retrial and that the Office of the Prosecutor intends to call the applicant as a witness at the retrial. The applicant then presents in support of this the rapporteur of the parliamentary assembly report which I'm reminded is the same report, I believe, that Mr. Rogers makes references to in his letter to the witness's attorney.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: That's not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Oh, this is a separate one. In that case, it's the Marty report, I expect.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: No, it's the Gardetta report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. Nice to know. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just so that you take me along, what document are you looking at at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry I'm looking at the second page of the (redacted), Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I've moved to the second page. And, really just going on down to the final substantive paragraph. The finding, as a result, essentially, I would say, apparently entirely of Mr. Rogers's letter:

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Now, this as I say, was provided to me at 1.52 today, as I was preparing to come into court, and we still, as Your Honours will see from page 1 of this small bundle, in relation to my first request, which I would have thought was perhaps the simplest one, any correspondence between the OTP and any other party such as the authorities, lawyers, or -- I'm sorry. We can now go back into open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I was just going to interrupt you. May the Chamber please move into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Yes, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I was saying. You will see from the reply received from the OTP just before we came into court, in relation to item 1, they are still looking into my request for any correspondence between themselves and any other party relevant to this case, essentially. I find it shocking, in the extreme, that this documentation has been withheld from us until I filed a further specific request yesterday in writing. One would have thought that Mr. Rogers would have been on his feet with all of these items in his hand before you yesterday and not simply handing over the one letter received -- that he had sent to the attorney in (redacted). I find it shocking that they are still at this stage looking into the request for further documentation that we have asked for. I find it shocking that there is apparently an entire witness file in relation to this witness of which the Prosecution must have knowledge and which they should have sought in order to provide the Defence with the information that we has asked them for -- as long ago as January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which they should have sought from?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Should have sought from the country's authorities, in my submission. There is clearly a mass of documentation in relation to this witness which affects not merely the credibility of the witness but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I hold no brief for the Prosecution, however, I just do want to find out from you if Rule 68 does impose such an obligation on the Prosecution to find information that it's not in its possession and to find it to be able to pass it on to you; or is the obligation that the information that's in their possession should be disclosed?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think I am right in saying, and I will confer with my colleagues if necessary, that requests had been sent to the Prosecution in addition to Rule 68 for any information in their possession or which, by the reasonable exercise of due diligence may come into their possession that could affect the credibility of any of their witnesses. I will check with my colleagues. But once that is made, that request, in that form, most certainly they're under a duty. I don't say that they're not under a duty under the plain wording of Rule 68 in the circumstances we have here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What you are saying still doesn't answer my question, Mr. Harvey. My question is: Whether it's your position that Rule 68 obliges them to go looking for information which is not already in their possession which they suspect might affect the credibility of the witness and find it in order to disclose it to you? Or is the obligation imposing a duty on them to disclose that which is already in their possession and which they know to be exculpatory.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do not believe that a Prosecutor exercising the due diligence which his code of conduct demands of him allows him -- that that duty allows him to sit there and only hand over that which he conveniently has in front of him or in his file, and to -- to fail to look for material that he reasonably suspects might be out there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thank you for clarifying your position, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith may be able to enlighten us further.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Since you asked the specific question about "within the possession of the Prosecutor," the answer to that question is: It need not be in his possession but it must be within his actual knowledge. So the standard here is within his knowledge. 68(A)(i) says: "Disclose to the Defence any material which in the actual knowledge of the Prosecutor may ...," and then it continues. So it's set forth not in terms of the issue of possession but in terms of knowledge. But I think Mr. Rogers would be hard-pressed to take the position that this was not within his knowledge. But I'm only responding to your specific question at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure. In any case, if we look at what Mr. Harvey was saying: [As read] "I find it shocking that there is apparently an entire witness file in relation to this witness of which the Prosecutor must have knowledge and which they should have sought in order to provide to the Defence with the information." Okay. You say he must have had knowledge. I take note of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: -- at this stage, the Defence is put in a position where we really have to consider whether to seek sanctions. We really have to consider what steps we are going to ask Your Honours to take. And, as you know, having come into possession of this literally minutes before coming into court I have not had a chance to speak with either of my fellow counsel on this, and we would wish, certainly, to confer about the most expedient way of proceeding. But right now, as I stand here, I feel that I have been deliberately deprived of information which the Prosecution knew that they had, could, and should have provided to me, and I am being subverted and most importantly my client's rights are being subverted in our ability to conduct a proper, effective, efficient cross-examination of this witness. So, Your Honours, I'm sure you would like to hear further from Mr. Emmerson, Mr. Guy-Smith, and, of course, from Mr. Rogers. But for my part, I would ask for some time, not a lot of time, but some time to confer with my colleagues and with my client, because I haven't had a chance even to speak to my client about this extremely important information and the manner in which it has come to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Harvey. I think so that we don't have repetition. I would rather you confer first before Mr. Emmerson and Mr. Guy-Smith talk.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Might I be heard on that subject?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Emmerson. Let me just finish with Mr. Harvey first. I would have thought it would be better if you conferred so that when you do come and address the Chamber, you have marshalled your submissions and your thoughts collectively, and so that you also indicate whether you would be -- are you in a position now to carry on with the cross-examination of the witness. I thought doing that, you could confer during the next break and maybe make your submissions at the beginning of the next break. That's a point I'm throwing at you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I understand the Court's desire to crack on, if I can put it that way. But with the greatest respect, I do not want to proceed one step further without conferring with my colleagues at least briefly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would you like a break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I would, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's hear what you wanted to say, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, two separate questions arise here. The first is the remedy necessary to enable these trial proceedings to remain on track. That is an issue about which we will undoubtedly need to confer. The second question throw and it doesn't matter which way around they come is: Having established the basic facts, is it appropriate at this stage to invite the Trial Chamber to exercise its powers under Rule 68 bis in relation to the imposition of sanctions. Now as to that, I don't need to confer. Can I just indicate to Your Honours what the position is and I'm going to invite us to go into closed session briefly so that we can have the chronology absolutely clear. Private session, briefly. And then, I will in due course invite the private session to be released publicly lest there should be any question that material is being withheld from the public. But I think, out of an abundance of caution, we ought to go into private session first because certainly in relation to one of these documents as Your Honours know, a submission has been made that it cannot be referred to in open session. I do not accept that submission and I want to address you in private session before you rule upon it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I just deal with the chronology, first of all. Before I do --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me give this warning. I think the Chamber at the end of the day is going to ask for a written motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm going to -- I've incorporated that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: To the extent that the you understand that it can obviate you going through the chronology now, it would save us a lot of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It doesn't obviate the necessity for setting out the reasons why and the basis for the nature of the order I'm going to ask you to make. Rule 68(i) is an obligation to provide disclosure which may affect the credibility of the witness but it is an obligation to provide that disclosure as soon as practicable. So it's no answer to a breach of Rule 68 that I've given it to you now, if it should have been given as soon as practicable at an earlier date. That is a breach of Rule 68. So the question for Your Honours to consider is not simply where are we now, but why are we where we are now, and should the Prosecution have given this disclosure at an earlier stage. Now you've heard various explanations from Mr. Rogers but I want this to be absolutely clear about the chronology and what remains outstanding. Yesterday you were addressed upon a letter from Mr. Rogers directed to (redacted), this witness's attorney in the immigration proceedings. You were provided with a copy of that letter, and as is clear from the letter itself, it is a letter from Mr. Rogers to (redacted) in response to an e-mail from (redacted) dated the 5th of November, requesting a letter concerning this witness. We have never received that e-mail, even now. So the request to which Mr. Rogers's letter responded has still not been disclosed but that is point one in this particular chronology. The 5th of November. On the 18th of November, clearly knowing that this letter was sought in response and in relation to an ongoing asylum application, Mr. Rogers wrote a letter that supported the asylum application. The next step is the e-mail dated the 2nd of February, so we've got a gap between the 18th of November and the 2nd of February. And the e-mail is directly to Mr. Versonnen from the witness saying that "one of your paper with information has been received by my attorney." One assumes since there's no other document being disclosed that the paper referred to is the letter from Mr. Rogers. And certainly that appears clear from the chronology. He goes on to say: [As read] "the information I gave to my attorney is like this: I told my attorney that my brother was killed in the war. This is not true. You know the truth. But I did this for the safety of my family in Kosovo and myself and my wife in the (redacted). "Now my attorney thinks that I am not telling the truth, which truth is that my brother was killed after the war." (redacted), and so forth. "My attorney is telling me why you did not tell me the truth." So here we have a situation where this witness having received his attorney having received Mr. Rogers' helpful letter in support of thinks then-refused asylum application is writing back to the Prosecutor saying I need your help. That's the last line of it: "My case here is in limbo I need your help for the safety of my life and my family." To which Mr. Versonnen responds, "We will keep you informed and bring it to the attention of the Prosecutor." Well, we've received nothing either subsequent to this to show what was done to keep him informed or what steps were taken thereafter. But what we do have is a document which is the judgement of the, as Mr. Harvey's pointed out to you, the (redacted), dated the 26th of August, which Mr. Rogers told me just before we came into court before Your Honours came into court, he had on Tuesday of this week. So all the way we were having the argument yesterday this was in the Prosecution's possession. This is an application by this witness's attorney, based upon Mr. Rogers's own letter for two alternative remedies: Reconsideration of the (redacted) previous refusal, to overturn the decision of the immigration judge, that application was refused; and alternatively, remand to the immigration judge to reconsider his decision in the light of Mr. Rogers's letter. That application was granted. In other words, the witness got what he wanted from Mr. Rogers. And from Mr. Rogers's letter. Namely, the overturning of a refusal of an asylum application. However, in that process, his own attorney was calling him a liar because what Mr. Rogers had said did not accord with what he had said to his attorney. I mean that is as far as one can divine the chronology. Yesterday, in what we submit was a dissembling attempt to justify the position of the Prosecution that the question of the asylum application was relevant to credibility because he had lied in it, but the assistance the Prosecution had given limb to have the decision overturned was irrelevant, Mr. Rogers tried to suggest that there was somehow no Rule 68 obligation on the Prosecution. That's why he was able to say, and Your Honours remember the passage, it is now 917, line 4, to 918, line 10, from yesterday which I had put into open session. Where Mr. Rogers led the witness in-chief on the lies or statements, rather, that he had made in the asylum application in order as he conceded to elicit evidence that was relevant to the witness's credibility. As Your Honours know, he left us in a situation where the witness had attested that he told the truth to the (redacted) when we all know that he lied, including Mr. Rogers. So that is the position. Now, going back over this history, there can scarcely be the slightest doubt that all of this material and all of these documents are part of the story relevant to this witness's credibility. It is not possible to distinguish between the lies he told to the (redacted) (redacted) and the deal he struck with the Prosecution to get him a letter assisting his asylum application which has now come to fruition just yesterday and which was in Mr. Rogers's possession while he stood up before you, making no reference to it, while we had an argument yesterday about the Prosecution's conduct in these proceedings. Going back to Rule 68(i): The obligation is to disclose as soon as practicable and that's why the chronology is important. The 5th of November letter from the lawyer. The 18th of November letter from Mr. Rogers. The 2nd of February letter from the witness himself saying his own lawyer is accusing him being a liar. The 2nd of February response from Mr. Versonnen. All of those documents should have been disclosed long ago and certainly the Prosecution cannot begun to argue that they have met their Rule 68 obligation to disclose this material as soon as practicable. Would go further and say given the obvious significance of the judgement was in existence and in Mr. Rogers' possession on Tuesday, he is in breach of Rule 68 (i) for not disclosing that while we had the argument yesterday. Can I just ask Your Honours to imagine what the situation would be if this material had all come to light at the end and after the trial? So says Mr. Rogers, well, if I was being naughty I wouldn't have given it to you in the first place. The duty is to disclose as soon as practicable. Mr. Rogers clearly does not either understand or take seriously his obligations of disclosure. The point is now being reached at which the Trial Chamber needs to consider the imposition of sanctions, and I don't need an opportunity to consult on that because it is absolutely clear. And so our application and the sanction that I would have in mind is a reprimand. Our application is for Your Honours to give directions now for the determination of a Rule 68 bis, a request for sanctions to be imposed on Mr. Rogers personally in the form of a reprimand for the manner in which he has conducted this disclosure exercise and the clear breaches of Rule 68 of which he has been guilty. If that is not done, given the entirely complacent attitude that Mr. Rogers continues to take to his continuing breaches of Rule 68 in relation to this witness, this Trial Chamber could not have any confidence with future witnesses some of whom raise very similar issues in very similar but perhaps even nor sensitive circumstances that Mr. Rogers with be trusted. Cannot be trusted in the exercise of his Rule 68 obligations. We saw that yesterday. What has happened here today is proof positive that that's the position. What possible explanation has he got for not disclosing a letter from the witness himself to the Prosecution on the 2nd of February of this year, asking for further help in his asylum application because what has been given so far has revealed him to his own lawyer to be a liar. That says Mr. Rogers, somehow, in la-la land that he lives in, isn't relevant to credibility. It's time to take a grip on the situation, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, are we in open or closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I would ask that we move into open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In addition to the application made by Mr. Emmerson, with regard to personal sanctions concerning Mr. Rogers's behaviour and performance, I would also remind the Chamber that there are legal remedies available to it at this point in imposing sanctions with regard to how this witness's testimony should be treated in -- in light of the specific Rule 68 violations that have, thus far, been established. Other than that, I join the remarks of my colleagues and because you've asked for brevity, I'm not going to go further with my comments at this time. Although I have a great deal to say. But at this time I'm going to be finished for now.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just add this. As regards the question of what should be in private session and what should be in open session, without referring to the nature of the document, as Your Honours know, Mr. Rogers has written a letter to the Defence disclosing a particular document from an official body concerning this witness, arising from the country in which is he is currently residing and the letter disclosing that indicates that the lawyer acting for the witness had been contacted by Mr. Rogers yesterday to inquire whether there was any confidentiality attaching to that document and: [As read] "He," that is the lawyer, "has informed us that this," the document, "should be treated confidentially and only referred to in private session, especially as the witness has not seen or been made privy to it himself." With respect that is it not a reason for private session. There is no reason why that document needs to be in private session. The lawyer concerned is not in a position to dictate whether it should or not be referred to only in private session. He has not asserted any kind of legal privilege. Had he done so, it would be spelled out in the letter. He is simply saying that because the witness has not seen it, it ought not to be referred to in open session. We disagree. There is no justification for that, and for that reason, the submissions that I made in closed session, subject to redactions of reference to the state concerned or any other identifying language should in due course be released into open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I would join in those remarks and based upon my experience in American practice, I don't believe there has been any basis on which is these matters should be alluded to in private session. As a general proposition, hearings are held publicly and transcripts are available for public review.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Yes, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was careful when I was reading from that document in private session to express myself in ways that could be made public following the application that Mr. Emmerson has just made. In other words, I believe I avoided any reference to the witness by name or to the country in question by name, and I therefore apply that that portion of what I read to Your Honours and that portion of our colloquy should also be made public. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harvey. Mr. Rogers, do you have any comments to make on everything that has been said this morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes. There's quite a lot that has been said. Your Honours, dealing with Mr. Emmerson's application, Your Honour, I would prefer to deal with that, given its highly personal nature, I would prefer not to deal with that orally but to deal with it by writing so that we can deal with the whole of the history fully and properly and set it out clearly in writing in that document. So far as the question of privacy, my understanding of that is that these documents are treated confidentially and in private in the state in which they come from. They're not publicly available. And to accord respect to that judicial determination that they are not publicly available, the reference to the documents should be in private session. The primary reason is not that the individual has not seen it himself, but that that is my understanding of how these documents are treated in the country, which is why I made the inquiry that I did before any disclosure of that was made. And, in addition, there is a question, and certainly it was an operative question in my mind, as to the relevance of it at that time. Subsequently, considering it only arrived on the day when the Chamber was not sitting, given where we are as a result of our discussions yesterday, I thought it right that the -- that document be provided to the Defence. Now, they seek to draw a conclusion from it, that, because something was provided for the individual and a result occurred, that there was some form of complicity in that outcome. That is simply not the case. Mr. Emmerson has very strongly suggested that there was some sort of deal. There was no deal and there never has been any deal with the individual in question. So I deal, then, with the e-mail, and that should have been disclosed; I agree. And as soon as it came to my attention on the review of this file, I -- which was this morning, shortly before we came to court, I instructed that it be disclosed immediately to the Defence, having looked at the document and clearly seeing the relevance, the relevance is clear, as a result of the discussion we had, which is why we provided it immediately to the Defence. It should have been on the delayed disclosure list. It wasn't. But it should have been. And as soon as I saw that that was an error, I corrected it, immediately, by sending it to the Defence. This is a delayed disclosure witness so the materials, any materials relating to him, were only due for disclosure on the 18th of July, subject to the order of the Court. And we did provide a lot of material to the Defence relating to this witness, including the material relating to his immigration status and the documents that Mr. Harvey referred to yesterday. They have had since then to make further requests and I understand the point that is made to Rule 68. But nevertheless they have had since then to make further requests relating to correspondence and information, et cetera, et cetera, concerning the application. And the first indication of that came from Mr. Harvey when the witness had already commenced his evidence in-chief. And since then, we have been trying to address it as fairly and properly -- I know my learned friends have said a great deal of personal things against me, but I have been trying to deal with it fairly and properly and have provided information in what I understand my obligations to be, and I have given that to my learned friends as quickly as I could. And it also was of concern to me that I had received, unsolicited, the decision of the requisite body but in circumstances where it wasn't clear to me, first of all, that I could even disclose it, and, secondly, whether it was relevant given its nature. My learned friends seek to draw connections but on one view the outcome of the witness's asylum status, still uncertain as it is, is not a relevant consideration. But in fairness, having reflected and reviewed, I thought it right that they had it, so that they could, and I expected what came, make the sort of allegations and accusations and applications that they have. It's because I provided it, a devil if you do, a devil if you don't. It's a question of whether it was done quickly enough. And I've tried to explain the reason why. They now have it and they can deal with it with the witness in such ways as they see fit. In relation to the question of lies, that was something that was brought up directly within the supplemental information sheet that was provided by the Prosecution to the Defence as a result of speaking with the witness during the course of the proofing that took place. Within that supplemental information sheet, the documents that Mr. Harvey, or at least some of the documents that Mr. Harvey has already identified, the witness speaks to those, and agrees that he did, in terms, agrees that he did lie on his immigration applications and the things that he said. That material, and the underlying material, was provided to the Defence back in July. That clearly goes to his credibility and was material that I provided to the Defence as quickly as could be provided to them. Your Honours, that's the position relating to the disclosure that I've given. I have answered a number of the requests that have been made, given that this request from Mr. Harvey was sent yesterday at ten past 6.00, of course, we're all still in court until 7.00 or just after 7.00. And then, as a result of the proceedings yesterday, there were quite a lot of things that I needed to discuss. So during the course of the morning we have been looking at that request. It is not straightforward. It is not normal for the Prosecutor to disclose correspondence with outside states or entities or any other body in relation to its activities in investigating these matters. So that is not a normal request and it's not normally ordered but I'm looking at it, to see whether -- to try to deal with the situation that has arisen. That is something that we can do in this case or not. But given that Mr. Emmerson has also made a further request, I think very shortly before we walked into court, so as he criticises me, so I suggest writing it before we come into court. That is also perhaps subject to criticism, requesting basically all -- I did print it. Now I can't put my finger on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It simply records the request that I made several times on the record yesterday as a result of the non-disclosure that has been occurring.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: [As read] "All communications and contact whatever between the Office of the Prosecutor and any individual, state, body, agency, or other organisation in respect of any witnesses in the case." That's a pretty big disclosure request. Your Honours can see how the Office has to deal carefully with requests for correspondence because they are so broad and wide-ranging, and are not often or usually relevant and generally are covered by Rule 70 privilege in any event. I just say that as a broad and general comment. The types of areas that we're moving into by the types of requests that are being made, and the Office has to respond sensitively, not just in this case but having regard to the effect in other cases, of the position that it takes. That takes a little while to coordinate. Where there is information that is clearly, that is Rule 68, we do provide it. I know we argue about that, and I've accepted that in relation to that one e-mail it should have been disclosed; I accept that. Earlier. But we do take the responsibilities seriously. As much as Mr. Emmerson wishes to paint us as cavalier, uncaring, or yesterday, I think, Janus-faced was the insult that I remember most clearly, that is not of the way I have ever conducted myself. And, Your Honours, we will look at the requests or deal with the response to the requests, as I have done throughout this case, as quickly and efficiently as I can, addressing the issues that my learned friend raise. What they don't, of course, tell you is the significant amount of exculpatory material that we have disclosed relating to witnesses. Some of it very significant, indeed. But that's all forgotten when it comes to picking on these pieces as they go through and make the type of broad and wide-ranging accusations that they do. Now, Your Honours may have to make a determination in due course. Mr. Emmerson's made his application and you'll have to decide what to do with it. But in order to answer fully and properly to it, he needs to put his application in writing and we will respond to it in writing and Your Honours will, no doubt, deal with it as you see appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The Chamber did indicate at the beginning of Mr. Emmerson's speech that we would like to save time and we'd like to have this in writing, and everything that has been said this afternoon and possibly even yesterday, that the Defence wants relief on, should be put on paper, let whoever has to respond, respond to it properly, let the arguments be clear to the Chamber what is, indeed, that the parties are complaining about and what relief they want, and let the likes of Mr. Guy-Smith have the opportunity to add what they couldn't add because they were constrained by brevity. And once that has happened, I think the Chamber will give its ruling. And I ask the parties to please put everything on paper, not only with respect to disclosure, but also with respect to what needs to go public that is private. And let it be identified clearly so that when the Chamber does give its order it knows what it's giving an order on. I think that's only fair that I have --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand that you've said, Your Honour. And in order to crystallise the issue and put it into writing, I would specifically request at this time at a minimum the November e-mail from (redacted) because it is a document that leave a huge hole in this entire discussion and it's a document now that has been raised on a number of occasions, and I would specifically request that the Chamber order Mr. Rogers to divulge that document to the Defence so that we can put it in writing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This is my problem. I don't know what that document is you're talking about, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It's the document that was discussed by Mr. Emmerson when he was dealing with the chronology of events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It's a document. It is a letter from -- from this witness's lawyer or an e-mail from this witness's lawyer to Mr. Rogers to which he responded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I think Mr. Rogers is playing a very dangerous game here, in terms of the way that he -- the way that he is bleeding out slowly the information that he has within his possession.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's not the intention at all. I know that's what my learned friend like to think. One of the reasons I have not provided a full answer to the correspondence question is precisely because I do not want to drip-feed letter by painful letter to the Defence. That's not the right thing to do. The right thing is to provide to them the full material that they are entitled to, not in an individual, bit-by-bit basis. That is why they have not had at this stage, the correspondence. There is a question about the relevance of the correspondence itself. In this case, I provided the letter. It's the letter that they're concerned about. That is the thing that started this all off and that is why the -- the letter to which it responds was not provided. Because the thing that matters is the alleged intervention by the Prosecution into somebody's asylum case. I don't accept the characterisation that Mr. Emmerson puts upon it at all. He seeks to gloss it as an intervention. It is certainly not. It was -- as I said yesterday, a neutral document that was used within proceedings by the lawyer, yes. But that wasn't the intention of the Office of the Prosecutor to assist, but merely to provide an account, as I said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rogers. I just want to say that Mr. Guy-Smith, in response to what you are requesting, make that request in the written document. Let Mr. Rogers respond to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand that, but I don't want -- I've said this before and I -- and I am beginning to believe at a certain level that I must have either trouble hearing or I'm a broken record. I do not wish to put the cart before the horse. I wish to be in a position to fully ventilate the issue with the Chamber. This is an issue which is extremely serious. And in order to responsibly deal with it in the fashion that the Chamber has suggested, which is in writing, I do not wish to be in a position where I am requesting disclosure in order to make the point. We have been in this situation -- we have been in this situation before with regard to other matters and without -- and I don't want to at this point compound or confound some of the difficulties that are going on in terms of some of the positions that have been taken by Mr. Rogers. I'm asking for a simple piece of disclosure so that I can intelligently address what I believe to be grave breaches of the Prosecutor's behaviour and the Prosecutor's obligation. To the extent that it is going to impact upon this Chamber's fact-finding process, I think it is important for me to have that information before I begin to essentially speculate as to what that might be. Mr. Rogers takes the position that I'm engaged in speculation and the Defence is engaged in speculation and he is pure as the driven snow. Well, if he's pure as the driven snow, then give us the information so that we're in a position to analyse it and make a determination about whether his representations here are, in fact, accurate or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, once again, I say to you, it is not possible for this Chamber at this stage to make a determination on that request. You will have to -- if it has to be that you allege in your written submission that there is further disclosure that the Prosecution is refusing with and you want to draw inferences from that. By all means, make those inferences and ask for the right remedy. You are also wanting us to put the cart before the horse.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm absolutely not [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Here's the chronology of what we're dealing with here, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are aware of that document and what do you want this Chamber to do? Pull it out of Mr. Rogers?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Tell him to do his duty. Tell him to act like a proper Prosecutor; that is what I'm asking this Chamber to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I just suggest with respect that we try to lower the temperature a little, have a little more light and little less heat on the situation. Because it's clear that there are strong feelings about what has occurred and I hope that Your Honours will understand that if there are strong feelings in the way that there are from experienced professional advocates, there's a reason for it. So perhaps we could just take a moment to -- to look at the sequence of events that we are dealing with right now. Because Your Honour says to me, to each of us on this side of the bar, Put it in writing. We have to go away now and have a consultation amongst ourselves about what should happen with this witness. Now the position at the moment is that Mr. Rogers is telling you that the letter he wrote was not an intervention in this witness's asylum application. That's his position. But just pause for a minute. We are saying, Give us the letter to which you were responding so that we can see whether you're telling the Chamber the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: If I just develop my submissions. I understand that Your Honour wishes to get to the conclusion. But I have to say, it's not a question of cart before horse. We may have to have this witness adjourned indefinitely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... That's true. But let me just stop you there, Mr. Emmerson. At this stage, when Chamber is asking you to make a submission, so that it can make an order, if you do want to get that letter at this stage you can get it by agreement from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You can ask him to give it to you [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... We've asked him to give it to us, he hasn't given it. So we're asking you to order it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Rogers, are you still refusing to give this letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. It's not a question of refusing to give it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you prepared to give it to them now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: It's a question of trying to deal with it in the round. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My question to you are you prepared to give it to them now? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Give it to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you for that. I'm sorry that it involved such drawing of teeth. Because as Mr. Rogers is concerned not to give drip-feed disclosure, piecemeal, letter by letter, but an comprehensive, honest and open approach to disclosure, I'm sorry that you were drawn into having to order that in this way. Can I just finish my submission. Mr. Rogers has acknowledged to you in the submissions he made a moment ago that he has been guilty of a breach of Rule 68. He has told you that the e-mail of 2nd February, as is obvious, should have been disclosed at the appropriate time. That is a breach of Rule 68, unequivocally the case. He is suggests that it only occurred to him on a review of the file, and he's going to have to explain that because the e-mail that responds to it from Mr. Versonnen says, "I will bring this to the attention of the Prosecutor." And, of course, the letter that it relates to was Mr. Rogers' own letter. So if he is saying to Your Honours he didn't know about the e-mail, he is obviously going to have to explain that. But be that as it may, even on his own position the only question that is going to arise on these pleadings is what sanctions should you impose. Because he accepts he is in breach of Rule 68. We do not accept that it is as confined as he would like it to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You will ask for your sanctions, your relief, the relief you ask, that you require in your submissions and the Chamber will consider that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. But Your Honours will understand that there are two, as I said to you at the very outset, there are two separate questions: What should you do about the way Mr. Rogers is behaving and, separately, how do we keep this trial on track? You just removed a problem because Mr. Rogers's complete recalcitrance to his duty has had to be the result -- had to be overcome with an order in which he wouldn't even give you a straight answer three minutes ago. We're now in the situation where there is also -- it's clear from Mr. Versonnen's response to this witness on the 2nd of February, he says, "We will keep you informed." There is obviously a whole lot of further correspondence that postdates that communication as to what was going on between this witness who was to quote, sir, his own e-mail, looking to the Prosecution for their help at that point. There's obviously more. It is obvious. Now are to go ahead with Mr. Rogers not yet understanding, still now, what his obligations are?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Emmerson, for that. I don't think you expect an answer from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see the relief with which you were able to breathe out and the horror you have at somebody else getting to his feet. I get to my feet only for this: To say, I think, now, with respect would be a good time for us to adjourn for a short time so that the Defence can confer together and with our clients so that perhaps we can allow the temperature in the courtroom to cool a little, so that we can shed some light and take the heat out and so that we can consider together, for instance, whether we're going to ask you to appoint a special master to supervise disclosure since we clearly are dealing with a Prosecution that does not understand the duty of disclosure. But that's one of the things that we will be considering, if Your Honours are kind enough to grant us an adjournment -- because we want to move this case ahead. We most certainly do. Our clients have been sitting for a long time waiting for this case to move ahead. But we do not want their rights violated in the process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We will then take a break and come back at 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, first of all, may I thank you for giving us time to consult together. Secondly, may I notify you that the Defence has now been provided with a copy of a document which contains the message that was sent apparently on the 5th of November, 2010, by the attorney in the country to Mr. Versonnen and it says at the top history this, Madam, has been replied to and forwarded, whatever that may mean and at the bottom, it indicates that this comes from Mr. Versonnen's computer dated yesterday but for whatever reason did not form part of the package that was turned over to us just before we came into court today. So we now have that. Your Honours, I have discussed this with my colleagues, I have discussed this with my client. As you recall, when we broke off yesterday, I was in the middle -- actually, I was far from the middle, I still beginning a review of this witness's conduct and statements to the country's immigration authorities. I am not in a position to proceed with any further questioning of this witness until I have full disclosure from the Prosecution. I believe it would be grossly prejudicial to my client's interest for me to ask him a single question more until I have full disclosure. I'm very confident -- very cognisant of the Tribunal's wish to get on, to move ahead, and if there were anything that I thought I could responsibly do as advocate for my client to move this case ahead with this witness, I would do so, but I ask you to accept from me my assurance as an advocate of almost 40 years that I have never been in a situation like this and I will not prejudice my client, with the greatest respect, by asking a further question of this witness until I have the disclosure to which I believe I am entitled. And we will, of course, be putting those matters in writing to Your Honours with all due speed. So that is my application: That the evidence of this witness should be postponed until we have full disclosure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I indicate, first of all, I adopt and endorse that approach. The document that Your Honours managed to elicit from Mr. Rogers just before the adjournment, if read in conjunction with Mr. Rogers' reply, we would invite you and will ensure that a copy is provided to you to draw the inevitable inference that there is only one reading of Mr. Rogers' reply which is that it was, indeed, a deliberate, knowing, and intentional intervention by the OTP in this witness's asylum appeal at the request of his lawyer. It is clear. Now the reason I say that is because, first of all, Mr. Rogers told you that it wasn't a few moments ago. And accused me of mischaracterising it as such whereas the document that has now been elicited confirms that that is exactly what it was. Secondly, because of what Mr. Harvey is applying for now is an opportunity to file written submissions, both on the question of sanctions and on the question of remedies because it is clear that there is a considerable body of further material relating to this particular witness which Mr. Rogers has still not yet had prized out of his hands. That being the case it would be wrong to proceed at this stage without the issues having been resolved about prosecutorial conduct, the consequences of that, both for Mr. Rogers but also more importantly for the conduct of the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, I really don't want to interrupt you in your address. Could the Chamber invite you to make all those submissions as part of your written submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Absolutely. But obviously the issue at the moment that Your Honours have to decide is whether or not the evidence of this witness should stop at this point until those questions have been ruled upon so it is important that you should understand that we -- it's not simply a backward-looking question as to what has gone wrong so far but a forward-looking question as in relation to this witness what is still yet clearly undisclosed and relevant material and more generally we are about to have a recess of three weeks. The joint submission will address structural defects in the Prosecution's approach to disclosure as exemplified by this witness. And is likely to invite the Trial Chamber to make certain -- order certain arrangements to be made to ensure it doesn't occur in the future. There is one further witness to be called in the present session who is the next witness in line. We are not inviting Trial Chamber to suspend that witness's evidence until the Prosecution can be put in a position where it conducts its duties properly, but I give notice now that the time-frame for submissions and a ruling will need to take account of the fact that it will be a firm submission of the Defence that this trial should not resume until the motions that are about to be filed and we will endeavour to file a single joint motion have been responded to and ruled upon because there are witnesses upcoming in relation to whom disclosure may be a very significant issue and in relation to whom, we would submit, it would be, given what has happened so far, wrong, for the trial to be permitted to proceed until a proper and responsible and professional disclosure responsibility has been put in place, to ensure that Mr. Rogers is not left as judge of his own cause. So, in other words, we are inviting Your Honours to suspend this witness's evidence. We are not inviting you to adjourn into the recess now. We would be content to proceed with the next witness because disclosure in relation to him is not an issue of such acute concern. This witness will obviously have to be recalled in the next session, but before the next session we would need to be clear and, certainly, we would be inviting the Trial Chamber to have ruled upon and decided these issues because it would be very wrong for this trial to continue with a Prosecution who can't discharge its disclosure obligations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Emmerson. Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith. I know you are renowned for brevity.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I request the matter with regard to this witness's testimony be adjourned until the resolution of written submissions. I join in the request made by Mr. Emmerson with regard to the presentation of the next witness's testimony so that we can meaningfully use the time that is left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Guy-Smith. Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, we clearly need to resolve these issues. I have no objection to the course of action that is being advocated by my learned friends. We can get on with the next witness. It is regrettable that this particular witness may have to go away and come back again, particularly having regard to the personal circumstances that he is currently under. However, I do think we need to resolve the matters that have been raised, and I would -- I would concur.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Rogers. In that event, I want to suggest the following course of action: That we move into closed session, invite the witness in, warn him about his obligations that he is still in the witness-stand, and then we can call the next witness. Is that okay? May the Chamber please move into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. You may be seated. Sir, you might be surprised that you've been sitting outside and not coming in to testify. There are a number of issues that have been raised by the lawyers. As a result of those issues that they have raised, it is not possible to continue with your further questioning. You are going to be excused to stand down from the witness-stand. You are not completely excused from further testifying. However, the issues that have to be resolved may take a bit of time, and I'm not sure what arrangements will be made, whether you will go home and come back or are you stay around here pending the resolution of these issues but what is of importance from our side is that you still on the witness-stand. You are still barred from discussing the case with anybody, in particular, with the Prosecution. You will stand down and until you are told to return to the witness-stand. And make sure that when you are called upon to come back, you avail yourself. Thank you very much. You may stand down. Until you hear from the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Rogers, do we still -- do we need to stay in closed session for the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Menon will deal with the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Rogers. Welcome, and good afternoon to you, Mr. Menon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. The Prosecution called Skender Rexhahmetaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. While we're waiting for the witness, Mr. Menon, how do you pronounce the witness's surname?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. The surname is pronounced Rexhahmetaj.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note it is pronounced Rexhahmetaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, madam.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the witness, Judge Delvoie seems to recollect that counsel for the Defence indicated that there is a document that is not in the Chamber's possession that you promised to let us have. And was wondering whether you would let us have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It's the document of the 5th of November e-mail to which Mr. Rogers responded. Yes, I have copies for Your Honours. In fact we collated them together with the reply. I know you already have the reply, but if I give you three sets. I am afraid they're not stapled. That's why I was sitting Your Honours, because I thought might want to have it stapled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We thought you might file them with the motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, they will come with the motion, but, I think to give Your Honours advance notice and to put the response in proper perspective, it might be an idea to see it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. Good afternoon to you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Menon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Sir, can you confirm for us that you're receiving translation in a language which you understand and are comfortable with. Sir?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you state your full name for the record, sir.

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Skender Rexhahmetaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And can you confirm -- and can you indicate what your date of birth is again for the record, sir.

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: I was born on the 13th of October, 1969.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, sir, what is your place of birth?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Isniq.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And in what country is that, sir?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: It's in Decan municipality, Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And, sir, did you provide the Office of the Prosecutor with a statement on the 24th of March, 2006?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And did you provide the Office of the Prosecutor at this Tribunal with another statement on the 24th of September, 2010?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And since you arrived in The Hague, sir, have you had a chance to review those statements in a language which you understand?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Yes, I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And did you review those statements in Albanian, sir?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, both of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, if we could call up 65 ter 03090. And, sir, are those your initials at the bottom of the page? Only the Albanian needs to be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 4 in both the English and the Albanian. Sir, is that your signature on the page in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, sir, can you confirm for us that this document captures the changes or - excuse me - the corrections which you had made to the statements that you had signed on the 24th of March, 2006 and the 24th of September, 2010?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Yes. This is the document that captures the corrections.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, sir, if questions were asked to you about the subject matters covered in the statements which you signed on the 24th of March and 24th of September, would your answers reflect what's in those statements as corrected in this document?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would move for the admission of 65 ter 03043, which is the witness's statement of 24 September 2010. 65 ter 03058 which is the witness's statement of 24 March 2006. And 03090, which is the list of corrections to those statements, Your Honour, signed by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Those 65 ter numbers, statements tendered are admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number, respectively, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 03043 will be Exhibit P297. 65 ter 03058 will be Exhibit P298. And 65 ter 03090 will be Exhibit P299.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: With Your Honours' leave I will read the 92 ter summary for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you. The witness is a former KLA commander from the village of Isniq in Decan municipality. Following the armed confrontation of the Haradinaj family compound in the Gllogjan in March 1998 steps were taken to organise a military defence of the witness's village of Isniq. The witness was appointed as a commander of his village defence. In organising the defence of his village, the witness and his fellow villagers worked with the KLA headquarters in Gllogjan. The witness went to the village of Gllogjan in the second half of April 1998 where he met Ramush Haradinaj for the first time. The witness gives evidence relating to a meeting which he attended in Gllogjan on 23 May 1998 and the military structure that was created at this meeting. The structure was comprised of five subzones. The witness was appointed as one of the subzone commanders. In his evidence, the witness describes the role which Ramush Haradinaj played within this military structure. The village of Jabllanice was not included within the five subzones that were created on 23 May 1998. The witness met Lahi and Nazmi Brahimaj for the first time at a meeting which took place in the first place in the first half of June, 1998. The witness had asked Ramush Haradinaj to organise the meeting with the Jabllanice KLA headquarters in order to improve cooperation with their village. The witness approached Ramush Haradinaj because he had better contacts with the Jabllanice KLA headquarters and knew those in Jabllanice better. The witness confirms that Ramush Haradinaj officially became the overall commander of the Dukagjin zone, including Jabllanice, on 23 June 1998. According to the witness, operations between the Gllogjan and Jabllanice KLA headquarters were coordinated on an ad hoc basis prior to 23 June 1998. The witness also gives evidence relating to Ramush Haradinaj's relationship with and authority over Idriz Balaj. That ends the 92 ter summary for this witness. I would ask, with Your Honours' leave, to show the witness 65 ter 01264.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And if the Albanian version could be shown to the witness and both the Albanian and English versions shown for the rest of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Sir, do you see the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this document is, sir?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: This document is a record, I would say, of -- or the minutes of a meeting that was held in Gllogjan in June.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, sir, do you recall what this meeting concerned?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: The letter contains the points to be discussed on the agenda. The first item is the establishment of the Dukagjini operational staff and the duties of the operation command and what we should do regarding the organisation of the formations, the staffs, the units, in that zone; and then another element is -- that was discussed in this meeting was the training of the units going from the individual to the collective training, and the engagement of the command for the preparation of the training programmes and issues of coordination among the units that would operate in the Dukagjini operational zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, sir, do you see your signature on this document?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Not on this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Maybe if you go to the second page in Albanian. Do you see your signature on this page, sir?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Yes, I see -- I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Beside which --

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: It's the sixth -- can you repeat the question again? I didn't hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Beside which number do you see your signature, sir?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Besides number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... is that the first reference to 6 on the document, sir, or the second reference to 6 on the indictment?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: I don't recall, but I know that that's the signature with my name, my last name, my position. I have written it myself, but I don't know whether it's the first or the second.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: No. I'm just -- do you see two references to the number 6 on the document, sir?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: The second one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Okay, thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P300.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Menon. Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Just one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Rexhahmetaj, I'm -- want to ask you some general questions about the emerging organisation and lines of command amongst the developing KLA during the period from March through to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. I think there is no interpretation in Albanian.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We know what the problem is. Is it because the interpreters are not interpreting or is it because they're not coming through? Mr. Court Usher, is the witness on the correct channel? Could somebody in the Albanian booth say something? Testing, testing. Let's hear whether the witness can hear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, now I hear. Now I hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Sorry about that, Mr. Emmerson. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
