utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Rexhahmetaj. We'll start again. I want to ask you quite a large number of questions over the next hour or so about the structures that gradually were put in place in the emerging organisation of the KLA in the Dukagjin zone, between March 1998 and September 1998, and about lines of command. So I'm just letting you know the sorts of topics that I want to ask you about. And so it won't always be necessary for you to give us vast amounts of detail. If you can listen to the question and try to answer specifically the question that I'm asking you, if it is necessary to ask you for further detail, then either I will ask you or the Judges will ask you for clarification. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So I want to take you back to the earliest part of this period, first of all, to March 1998. Now, at that time, were you living in Isniq?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So can we take it that you were in the Dukagjin zone consistently from March 1998 through to September 1998?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say that you had a good grasp from information that was provided to you from a variety of different sources, a good grasp of what was taking place in the organisation of the Kosovar Albanian community?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Yes, I had. I was informed of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And a good grasp, also, of the emerging structures that came into operation within the KLA in that area.

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Yes. I had a good grasp, beginning from April, actually, when I assumed the responsibility for my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Let me start, then, by asking you of how you came to assume the responsibility for your village. I just want to get a sense, so the Judges can get a sense, of how this type of thing was happening. So let me ask you some specific questions. During the course of March, is it right that there were three attacks by combined Serbian forces on families associated with the Kosovo Liberation Army, firstly the Jashari in Prekash; secondly, the Tahirsylaj family in your own village of Isniq; and then, thirdly, the Haradinajs in Gllogjan?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Yes. Your information is accurate regarding the events. I want to explain, however, that during the attack on the Tahirsylaj family it occurred at the end of January 1998. Then we have the attack on the Jashari family. Everybody knows what happened. And then we have the attack on the Haradinaj family, on the 24th of March in Gllogjan.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification about the order and the dates, and that's a good example of when additional detail is helpful. Now, first of all, I want to put a specific suggestion to you, a series of specific suggestions. At that time would it be fair to say that the Jashari family and the Haradinaj family were two entirely independent pockets, neither -- of KLA activity, neither one commanding the other?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: At that time where specifically? In March or for the entire period, March to September.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No, no, no. At that time, I meant March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: March.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Geographically speaking, Drenice and Dukagjini or Decan are far away. But these families were, of course -- lived in different locations. Militarily speaking, there wasn't any connection between them. They were simply attacks mounted by the forces of Serb occupiers against Albanian families.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'll come back to the attacks and their aftermath in a few moments. But, first I want you to give the Trial Chamber a sense of these different concentrations of KLA activity and how they related to each other. So the question I want to put to you specifically is, that there was no command structure by which the Jasharis commanded the Haradinajs, or the Haradinajs commanded the Jasharis, was there?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: No, there was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And, similarly, we know from other evidence that the Brahimajs had a concentrated KLA base in Jabllanice. They weren't commanding the Jasharis, were they?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: To my knowledge, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: They weren't commanding the Haradinajs either.

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: No. No, they weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So that the Chamber has the picture, you had pockets or groups of people belonging to the KLA but within -- all operating -- maybe speaking to each other but all operating with essentially separately around their family bases. That is, up to the time of the attacks that we discussed.

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: You are talking about the time of the attacks? During those months? I have no information or accurate information on the military organisation because that didn't exist as such. They were separate groups. I don't have information. I have no knowledge whether they had any links. But I think it was very difficult for them to have any links at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So I understand you might yourself not know of any possible communications or anything of that kind on a limited level you may not have any detailed knowledge. But you said to us just now, the military organisation, that didn't exist as such. They were separate groups. Can you just expand on that briefly, in your own words.

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: In the past periods, I was not involved in this. I wasn't part of any political or military group. My involvements in the Kosovo Liberation Army or the first armed groups dates back to the beginning of April 1998. So I have no information about the existence of such groups, their number, the way they operated. I wasn't there, part of them, as I said. So my military activity begins in early April 1998. It is from this period onwards that I can speak. Prior to that period, I can give you nothing. Because I have no information.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll -- I'll just ask you one further question on this. When you said they were separate groups and the military organisation didn't exist as such in March, prior to the attacks, can you tell us what you meant by that?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Later on, in the later periods, I understood that there were small groupings that were active in the 1990s. But personally I did not belong to any of these groups. I don't know how they functioned. But later on I received information that there were such small groupings in the 1990s that were active then.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in your particular village, in Isniq, the attack on the Tahirsylaj family was an attack that had a profound effect on the village and the surrounding areas; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Yes. It was an attack mounted by the police forces, supported by armoured vehicles, and they surrounded the compound of the Tahirsylaj, and, as a result, there were two or three people who were injured.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Injured or killed?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: After their compound was surrounded, a few hours later, the Serbian police got into the house and arrested two people. This was an attack at the time when the Serbia repression had reached very large dimensions, and they, now, did not attack only young people or individuals on the street but families. This was another stage of the Serbian repression on Albanians in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, shortly after that attack, you've told us about the Jashari family attack. In that attack, is it right that a large family was literally wiped out, with every living person, from male adults to babies, being killed?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. All the people there, men, women, the elderly, children, babies were not spared. This was a very horrible event, and it is known all over the world now, what the Milosevic forces and policy did to the Albanian families.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: What I'm particularly want to ask you about is what effect that had on the communities in western Kosovo. But, first of all -- just wait for the question. First of all, people regarded it and described it, did they not, as a massacre?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: The Prekash event shook the whole public opinion in Kosovo and in the western democratic countries. And from that time on, the population in Kosova felt very unsafe and very concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And in broad terms, did that then lead to a general perception on the ground that there was a necessity for communities to arm and defend themselves against similar attacks?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: It was exactly these horrible events that we just mentioned made the Albanian population to -- sit down and think, to find the form of protecting themselves from these notorious attacks mounted on them by the Serbian police and army forces. So the civilian population could not find any other means to protect themselves rather than just protect themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Focussing on your own village, in Isniq and perhaps the surrounding villages, is it right that after the attack on the Haradinaj family compound, the next one in line on the 24th of March, is it right that, after that, young men from your village travelled over the mountains and into Albania to bring back arms and weapons for your own village?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: After these events, there were initiatives taken by small groupings of young people in Isniq who were seriously thinking that they had to face such situations in the future, because we had one such event in Isniq that had already happened. Then the Gllogjan attack happened. And ordinary people knew that the situation would become even more complicated, and that's why small groupings of young people, young men went to Albania to procure, to get weapons for self-defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, at the time that those groupings of young men went, the time they left Isniq to go to Albania, it's right, isn't it, that there was no organised KLA in your village of Isniq at that time.

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: No. At that time, there wasn't. These were the first steps. It was -- it was the initiative of ordinary people who felt they had to defend themselves, and that's why they took it upon themselves to go and get supplies of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And did there come a time soon after that attack on the Haradinaj compound, did there come a time when there was talk in the village about trying to organise a village defence, i.e., not just having pockets of individuals with guns who had been brought in from Albania but actually trying to organise a village defence for Isniq?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Yes. There were such initiatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And in that process of trying to organise the Isniq village defence, I mean, it's right, isn't it that initially, at least it wasn't a KLA village defence. It was just the village defence.

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That's how it went. It was the logic of self-defence, self-protection. There was initiatives and opinions that were expressed with regard to how to be able to face further attacks by the Serbian forces because ordinary people were very concerned about the future fate. And that's why young people took such initiatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Pausing there for a minute, and still focussing on this period of time, when the first steps were taken in Isniq to organise a village dense, would that be at the beginning of April?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Yes. It was early April. In the beginning, there was a small group that brought arms. By the end of March, if I'm not mistaken, it was either the 27th or the 28th of March. There were four weapons that were brought by a group of four people to Isniq, but, at the time, I was not aware that they existed. It was on the 2nd of April, or 3rd of April, that I became aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm going to come to that, then, in just a second. But just before we move on from that early period where the village was -- young people in the village were bringing arms and there were attempts to set up a village defence, just focussing on that period for a moment. You've told us people were frightened. It's right, isn't it, that Isniq was particularly impacted by the attack on Gllogjan because, is it not right that the civilian population of Gllogjan, many of them came into Isniq on 24th of March when they were fleeing from the Serb attack?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Yes. The attack on Gllogjan frightened people. And each village, the population of the villages generally began to think seriously about defence, as a result of the attack on the Haradinaj family in Gllogjan. And, at that time many civilians from that village came to take shelter in our village, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And when you say "at that time," you mean at the time of the 24th of March, when the Serbs attacked Gllogjan, many of the civilians from Gllogjan tried to take refuge in Isniq. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And so you said that in the first few days of April, I think you said the 2nd of April, or the 3rd, you became aware for the first time that within your own village there were youngsters with guns; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And did you become aware of that because you yourself were approached to ask whether you would help try and organise a village defence?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: I was told by one of my cousins that there is a small group of people who had weapons in the village, and they had asked him to ask me whether I would be willing to help them and support them in organising the defence of the village and -- in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: These people had no uniform, did they?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: No, they didn't. They were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And they were not claiming to be representatives of any army, were they? At that time.

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: No, they weren't. They were just people who were concerned about the fate of the population of the village and they wanted someone to lead them in defending the village. And when they had talked amongst themselves, they had decided that I was the person who was able to lead them.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And -- and the reason for that, as it was explained to you, was it because you had -- yourself had military training and a short period of military activity within the JNA?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Yes, correct. I graduated the Military Academy. I had relative experience in the army. And they thought that I would be the most appropriate person to support them.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now -- and you took up that invitation and agreed to be the leader of the village defence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Yes, correct. The moment I heard that they had expressed a wish for me to lead them and learned from my cousin that they had four weapons, three Kalashnikovs and one rocket-launcher, I accepted their proposal to be their leader, and, at the same time, recommended to them that, as they had decided to defend the village, they had to bring more weapons to the village at the shortest time possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And did you have a view as to whether there should be secrecy?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Of course. I recommended that there be secrecy, and I told the person who contacted me that, "You have not talked to me about this."

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So even within the village, it wasn't known that you and these youngsters were trying to organise a village defence; is that right? You had to keep it secret even within the village.

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, it's normal that secrecy should be kept.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: That really you don't - can I put it this way and see if you agree with it - that you would not want more people to know what you were doing than was strictly necessary. A need-to-know basis.

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: At the beginning, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, can we take it that men from your village, at your suggestion, did go and get more weapons?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. In the following days, there were small groupings that went to get supplies of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, pausing there for a minute and changing focus away from the attempt to arm certain people in the village, was there in Isniq, as in all other villages in Kosovo, a structure within the village by which community decisions were taken? A group of village leaders, in peacetime, as well as in wartime?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Yes, there was a structure. Life was organised in the village, and there was a chairmanship of the village that regulated life there; in difficult times especially.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: That's how society in Kosovo was and, to some extent, still is organised; is that right? With village leadership groupings chosen by the community.

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Yes, correct. It is a well-known fact that we have been through very tough times, so people tried to find ways to organise their life in the conditions of an occupation.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And obviously these leadership structures in the village, they're quite independent of any state structure imposed on Kosovo at that time by Serbia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Yes, of course. They were quite independent from the Serbian government. But, at the same time, I should add, they were at risk. The people in these committees were at risk, from the Serb government. Because they did not obey the state mechanisms or state structures, and they tried to organise life in the village, in order to have a modicum of normality in the villages. There were certain councils that were created in each and every village, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. In addition to that, it's right, isn't it, that these village command structures - I don't mean the military command structures, I'm talking about the village leadership groupings - that they were independent of one another so the village leadership in Isniq would be operating completely independently of, say, the village leadership in Prilep. They fought, if you like, they were concerned about the interests of their own people in their own village, and perhaps the surrounding villages. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So what I want to explore with you now is the relationship between this -- when this little village defence that you were trying to set up and the village leadership. Did you have discussions with the civilian leadership in Isniq about the village defence? Did you talk to any of them. You told us it needed to be kept secret. Did you talk to the civilian leaders of the village about what you were doing in Isniq?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Yes. Later on, I had meetings with them after I learned that there were weapons in the village, and after the recommendation I made for more weapons to come, after the second group and the third group went to Albania to get weapons and the weapons came, I was invited to a village Oda, to the council of the village, where we discussed the issues further, because, at the time, there had come over 28 weapons, so we could arm a platoon with them. At this stage, I would say that we could have a better organisation, and I thought that the village elders or leadership had to be informed about the ways we thought of organising the defence of the village, and that's why this meeting was held.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So it was held to inform them. Were you also asking for their approval or consent?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: There is no interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do we have a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: There's a technical problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do we have a technical problem somewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now there is interpretation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Sorry, the question I was asking you was: You told us you went to inform the village elders. Did you also go to seek their approval or consent to what you were doing in Isniq?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: In reality, at that meeting, on the 12th of April I think it was, when the young people had brought considerable amounts of weapons, I recommended that three members of the village council be present, in order for us to sit down and talk about what we were going to do in the future. Because this was a stage where things were getting more serious and we had to consult the village elders, in order to decide jointly and to get their approval and the approval of the whole population for defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And just to be absolutely clear, you needed to consult with the village elders and get their approval from the village elders in Isniq, but you wouldn't have sought the approval of the village elders from any other town or village, would you? It was your village elders that you needed to have the agreement of; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: I didn't need to get the approval of the elders of another village. The way life was organised in the village, it was independent [Realtime transcript read in error "wasn't dependant"]. And it was the beginning, as well, so the people who had been appointed as village elders had to be informed, consulted, and their approvals sought so that we could decide what to do in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I know some of these questions may seem obvious, or the answers may seem obvious, Mr. Rexhahmetaj, to anybody who has lived in Kosovo all their lives, but they're not necessarily obvious in the context of international Judges and lawyers looking at the structures in Kosovo, just to explain why I may be asking you questions to which the answers seem very obvious to you. Now, if that is the position, would you agree with me that, as you were forming your village defence, you were not taking instructions from anybody outside Isniq?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. These were only the very beginnings of our organisation because the population, the Albanian population, did not have its own government. We did not have our own state. So we were obliged under the conditions of the increasing repression to self-organise, and these were just the beginnings of our organisation, and they were independent of each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm -- it's pointed out to me there is a transcription error at page 60, line 6, where the transcript reads: "The way life was organised in the village, it wasn't dependant," and it should, of course, it was independent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. On that note, Mr. Emmerson, would that be an opportune moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It would, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: On that note, we will take a break and come back at quarter to. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may -- I beg your pardon. May we get the witness in, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I can't do it on my own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may be seated, sir. Thank you very much, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Rexhahmetaj, do you have translation?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, the picture that you've painted for us about Isniq and the start of an attempt to organise village defences there, can you tell us, please, from your own knowledge, it's right, isn't it, that the same sort of pattern was taking place in all of the villages in that area, of the formation of local village defences?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, the same pattern was applied in terms of organisation, which means that it was a matter of individual forms of organisations in each village.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: All operating independently of each other with no central command; correct?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, Isniq was fortunate in that it had a former JNA officer living in the village, namely you, and there were other villages that had individuals with military experience, such as Rrustem Tetaj; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Yes, correct. Rrustem Tetaj, too, was a former JNA army officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But there were lots and lots villages in the area who had no individual with military experience in the JNA living in the village, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And there, in those villages, it would just be a farmer or a local village leader who was put in charge of military defence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. In those villages where there were no trained officers or soldiers, the inhabitants decided of their own free accord on their own leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I want to focus with you now on the period between the middle of April and the end of May. That's the period I'm going to ask you about now: The middle of April and the end of May, okay?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: All the questions I'm asking you now concern that period. First of all, it's right, isn't it that around about mid-April, weapons started to come across more frequently and in larger numbers?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: That's right. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But still without any central organisation of these different and independent village defences.

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you to repeat your question, because I wasn't clear about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, let me -- let me put the question in stages. First of all, there was one incident, want there, one well-known event when as many as 120 young men travelled across the mountains and brought a large amount of weapons back to different villages in the Dukagjin zone. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: That's correct. But it cannot be called an incident. It was an initiative, to go and get weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Sorry, that's just a linguistic issue. So we have the picture correct, that in the second half of April and the beginning of May, there were large numbers of weapons coming over the border being taken to a large number of different village defences in different parts of the Dukagjin zone; correct?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And, at the same time, is it right that the Serbian forces in the region were accumulating?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: That is correct. If you allow me, I would like to make a minor explanation. Initially, the Serb regime chose to send police forces, but these forces were well-equipped, capable of conducting also military operations. We saw less of military forces at that time, but they were in readiness. We have no confirmed information but we know that, at that time, there were also army officers who were donned -- in police uniforms among the members of the police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: We -- I won't ask you a lot about the Serbian deployment because we have other evidence about the build-up of Serbian forces in western Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And for Your Honours note, that is particularly in the evidence of Colonel Crosland, which has been admitted by agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But it's right that the Serb forces in western Kosovo had overwhelming fire-power as against the village defences?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Correct. It was much larger fire-power than what we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say this: That really what was facing you in Isniq and other leaders in other villages at that time, was a choice between shooting back in the hope that you would keep the Serb forces out, or just letting them rampage through the village and massacre the entire population. Is that how you saw it?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Our aim was to make our best -- to make it impossible for the Serb forces to penetrate our villages who definitely aimed at massacring and decimating the civilian population. That was our objective at the time, our main objective.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But given the build-up of Serbian forces and given the additional number of weapons that were in the hands of various village defences, was it your view, your own opinion at that time, the end of April, that it was necessary to get some sort of coordination between these different village defences?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Yes. According to the military rationale of action, that was the case. This is what we did. There were also demands by the elected representatives of the villages sent to us, in this case to me, and they asked me when -- to help them regarding organisational experience, to form units or -- or staffs for the villages and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And so, was it then at the end of April, when you started to make contact with the commanders of the village defences in the other villages, such as Rrustem Tetaj?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Yes. There were village representatives who came for consultation. As I said earlier, I, on my part, I saw it necessary after we had formed the staff in Isniq on the 15th of April to study the ways of how I could contact the others so that we had better coordination in case of any eventual attack so that we could provide reciprocal assistance to one another.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think it's probably right to say, isn't it, that, at the time, in the end of April, in light of what had happened in Gllogjan on the 24th of March, the Haradinaj family were thought of as having a special reputation because they managed to beat the Serb attack on Gllogjan; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: It is right. That family had a reputation, because it was the first time for us to see a family managing to put up a resistance to the Serb forces. So it gained a good reputation by so doing among the population. And it was in light of what happened in Gllogjan and our efforts at self-defence that I took the initiative to contact the relevant people in the region to coordinate work among us, since my village and the region were at the preparatory phase, and lacked the next experience in case of any eventual attacks, whose size we didn't know at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And just answering yes or no, is it fair to say that the success of the Haradinaj family on the 24th of March in repelling the Serb attempted attack on the village, was an inspiration to other village defences?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And then was it with that in mind that, at the end of April, you first made contact with Ramush Haradinaj?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Yes. This was the reason why I did so. I don't remember very well, but I think this happened in the second half. In the beginning of the second half of April, during which time I insisted on meeting him and together with other members of the staff, we went to visit Ramush Haradinaj in Gllogjan.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And you went there because you thought that it would be a good idea for these various village defences to try to coordinate, and you wanted to discuss that with Mr. Haradinaj; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: That is correct. Coordination was one of the reasons, as I said earlier, we were at the beginning of our organisation. They had more experience than us, and we wanted to be ready for any eventuality, in case of any Serb attacks. So having a horizontal form of coordination was, in my opinion, necessary at the time. So to make sure that we didn't continue with our isolated forms of organisations but be in a position to provide mutual assistance to one another; that was the main reason and aim.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And is it right to say when you asked Mr. Haradinaj, when you came with your proposal to Mr. Haradinaj at that first meeting about coordination, that his response to you was that it may be too early, because some of the villages just weren't sufficiently organised themselves to be able to start talking in terms of a coordinated defence, at that time?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: It is correct. Yes, in the meeting we had together, he said that we, as a village, but this applied to other villages as well in the region, we should continue our efforts at organisation but that every exposure of ours might jeopardize our resistance from the start. Therefore, he was not in favour of making it very obvious, but would step up our efforts so that in the near future we would find the best way and the best form of organisation. I have to say, that, irrespective of the circumstances, he said that in case of any danger to the population, we should -- he should try to find the ways to help us as much as he could. But try to avoid an early exposure so that we didn't draw the attention of the Serb forces to our resistance and which would ensue on an attack against us.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just give us a flavour of these discussions with Mr. Haradinaj. I mean, can I put a proposition to you? These were discussions between two men, yourself and him, I mean, I appreciate there were others there, but these were discussions between two men looking to find a cooperative way forward; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: That is right. I was welcomed there, as I said earlier, I went there together with the staff. We were about ten persons, and he received us very well, indeed, and our discussion was sincere, our exchange of views, and we came out happy with the outcome of the meeting, even though we didn't realize the aim we went there for. However, we left content, and we went back to our village.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: In fact, if we could just move further in time to -- to the 23rd of May now, a few weeks later on, during those three weeks between the end of April and the 23rd of May, attempts to organise had continued; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Yes, yes, they continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The level of threat of attack from the Serbs had increased, as you understood it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And more of the villages in the area managed to establish some sort of rudimentary village defence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can we call up, please, P78. And then can we enlarge the central section.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: First of all, just to give you a moment to look at the map and the markings on it, just to familiarize yourself with the various locations. You can see -- can you see Jabllanice? Don't mark the screen at the moment because it will show on the map. But can you see where Jabllanice is? It is in a red oval mark?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And you can see the main Pec-Decan-Gjakove road running north/south on the left side of the map?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And can you please point us to Isniq, your village?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would you like the usher to help you.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Perhaps you can just put a circle around your village?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the usher please help you.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just give us a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: If we go back.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just bear with us for a moment, Mr. Rexhahmetaj. Now would you circle Isniq, please.

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And can I indicate just for Your Honours benefit, you'll hear or there is reference in the evidence to Irzniq, which is a different place from Isniq. Just an important point for you to realize.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If that is the case, may I just mention that what we have been seeing on the transcript is Isniq, I-s-n-i-q.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, that will do, because it doesn't have an R after it. Obviously there is an Albanian and Serbian spelling of each village. But Irzniq is a different village from Isniq or Istinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, just pausing there for a moment, Mr. Rexhahmetaj, on the 23rd of May, is it right that a meeting took place in Gllogjan, where for the first time the representatives of these different village defences in this area of western Kosovo all came together to discuss the possibility of organisation?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And, of course, organisation had been, if I can put it this way, a priority for you, hadn't it? It had been something you felt strongly about.

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: It was a priority and a necessity.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And I'm going to ask you some questions about a later period. But, generally speaking, is it right that throughout the period we're talking about, May to September, throughout that period -- I'm sorry, March to September, you were always pushing for greater organisation whenever you could.

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But it wasn't easy to organise any of this, was it, Mr. Rexhahmetaj?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: It was a very complex issue. It was difficult to organise. It took time. Because, in addition to organisation, we had to face the war. It was a burden on us, but with the passage of time, step by step, we managed to set up the structure to empower the defence and so on. This was dictated by the objective possibilities we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Limited by the reality on the ground; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: We'll look at some of those realities in the questions I'm going to ask you, and how they limited your capacities for organisation in the context of command structures. But, first of all, I want to focus on that very first meeting where everybody came together in an effort to try to, for the first time, impose some sort of coordinated structure. If you look at the map, can you see the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4 written on the map? Don't mark it for the moment. But can you see they're written on there -- you see those? And you see the areas that those numbers relate to? Can you see those?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now just for your information, this is a map that was -- those markings were put on this map by Rrustem Tetaj describing the approximate boundaries of the subzones that were agreed to be set up at that 23rd of May meeting, okay?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, I'm not asking you to change the boundaries or comment on any details of whether they're exactly correct. But broadly speaking, at that meeting was it agreed to try to organise the villages into four subzones, or five subzones, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Yes. It was agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: We'll look at the fifth subzone in a minute. But just focussing on subzones 1, 2, 3, and 4, subzone 1 is the area in which Gllogjan was situated; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And was it agreed at that meeting that that would be regarded as one subzone with the leader being Ramush Haradinaj?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it was agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Subzone 2 is the area in which the village of Irzniq fell, is that correct, or Rznic?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Irzniq, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And was it agreed that that would be set up under the subzone command of Shemsedin Qeku?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Subzone 3, which included Gornja Luka and Donja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Which Your Honours can see as "D. Luka" and "G. Luka" in the top left-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Subzone three, that was under the command of Rrustem Tetaj, is that right?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Right, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And, of course, subzone four, you were the village commander of Isniq. Who decided that you should become the subzone commander for the whole of subzone 4?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: I would like to take a while, if you allow me to explain, to explain the procedure of selection. We were invited, two representatives of each village staff, local staff were invited to attend the meeting at Gllogjan at that time. And from Isniq, and from all the villages that were involved in the war, and which might be potentially involved were invited. I cannot be accurate about the exact number of villages present there. Maybe between 20 and 30. We met at an Oda which is a room where we went through two rounds of selection, three actually, to come up with a structure at a horizontal level. This is how I described it then, and how I'm describing it now. Horizontal command. During the first round --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Sorry, just pause there. What do you mean by "horizontal command"?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: By that, I mean when there is no vertical command chain. In my opinion, that was -- that was horizontal. Horizontally spread in terms of command. We had five commanders appointed for five subzones, and they were unanimously elected by the representatives of the local village staffs of all the villages present at that meeting. In the first selection round, the representatives of the villages could discuss among themselves, there were two from each village, and they agreed who would take part in the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: This is the procedure -- the procedure that really happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I just ask you to pause for a minute because we could go through a lot of detail. Could I try to take it a little shortly. First of all, this meeting, how long did it take from start to finish?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: I can't be sure about the exact time. Over two hours, I think. Because the procedure itself, the selection procedure, selecting the people who lead them, us, took long. I can't be precise about the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And because it is going to become important in due course. And the process by which these decisions were made were they made with everyone having a say in the Oda sitting around in a circle in a large room with only men?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And everyone expressing their opinion one by one?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And then decisions being reached by consensus and agreement.

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No one was telling anybody else from any other village or area what to do or how to organise, were they?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: There was no dictate. The will of every village was taken into consideration during the selection process, to elect the people, you know, that would be in command. This is to cut a long story short.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: The will of the representatives of the villages were taken -- was taken into consideration, to -- to elect the people who would lead the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And -- and, again, so that the Judges have the picture, was that generally how decisions were always made within the KLA during the period March to September, by decisions in which everybody had a voice and then a position was reached by agreement? Or --

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Yes. The decisions were taken like that. Generally, every decision that was taken and every selection of a structure that was made within the KLA in the Dukagjin operational zone was done through expressing the free -- each person expressing their free will and respecting the will of the individual himself. Nothing was imposed on anyone. If I, for example, did not want to take on a certain responsibility, I could refuse, and somebody else was appointed. But it was our collective will to do what we could to do our best to have a structure in order to have a successful resistance towards the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: That's helpful. But -- but just to take it one stage further, so that the Judges can understand why that would be and why this would continue to be the position, I mean, is it fair to say that, first of all, that there was no state or legal authority behind any of you?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. We did not have a state at all, as you all know, and the situation imposed upon us, this participation in war, and all this organisation was occurring because people wanted to defend themselves and the Kosovan people were under threat. The threat of whether they were going to exist anymore or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Rexhahmetaj, can I just make one general comment. This is not a criticism at all because your evidence is extremely important. But your answers are getting a bit longer as we go on. If you could just try to keep them a little shorter, and if I need to ask you a second question, I will. Because, otherwise, we've got quite a lot of material to get through. Is that -- I hope you won't take that rudely.

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So given that you had no legal authority behind you, is it right to say that throughout that period that we're concerned - with March through to September - getting individuals to do what you needed them to do was always about consent and persuasion, rather than the issuing of orders that could not be enforced?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: The only form was by consent. In taking decisions, we operated by consent because we did not have any legal power or any authority given to us by a state in order to give orders to anyone. We wanted to help. We wanted to help our homeland, our people, and on these sound bases, we wanted to have decisions based on consent and consensus, not by imposing orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You mentioned that there's a fifth subzone which is not shown on this map. Is that the subzone that was established around Voksh and Drenoc under the command of Adem Ukehaxhaj?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Yes. This was the fifth zone. I apologise, but I don't know the exact villages included in the zone. I know that Voksh was one of them and the commander of that zone was Adem Ukehaxhaj, who was a career officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So the judges have it clear, I'm not going to ask you to mark it because you don't know the precise villages, but that subzone was on the west side of the main Pec-Decan-Djakovica -- Gjakove road?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And we've heard evidence from Bislim Zyrapi, that when he visited in July, that zone was so cut off from the subzones on the east side of the road that it could not be effectively incorporated. Is that your recollection?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Menon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honours, just a clarification. I believe that Mr. Zyrapi testified that he did not visit the village of Voksh.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: His testimony was that he visited that subzone on the west side of that road, that it had been impossible to incorporate it because of the communication disruption caused by Serb military manoeuvres and presence on the main Pec-Decane-Djakovica road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Perhaps Mr. Emmerson can put the reference to the specific area that Mr. Zyrapi refers to in his evidence because it's [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I obviously can't do that on my feet. Let me ask the witness his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just looking at your own knowledge of the situation, Mr. Rexhahmetaj, the subzone that existed on the west side of the main road, is it right that that subzone was physically and militarily cut off? And you can answer that question yes or no for the time being.

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Yes, you can say that it was cut off. Isolated.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, after the meeting on the 23rd of May, I now want to concentrate on the period of time between that meeting on the 23rd of May when these subzones were set up and another meeting that took place on the 23rd of June in Jabllanice, so it is that period I want to concentrate on. And you remember Mr. Menon took you to a document dated the 24th of June in your evidence earlier on this afternoon, concerning the appointment of different commanders. Do you remember seeing that document?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: The document I was shown earlier is a simple document. And I remember the time when we signed it. The aim of the signing was to confirm that we attended the meet.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, I'm not asking you about that document at the moment. I want to ask you about the period of time, the month, that took place between the establishment of these four subzones on the 23rd of May, and the meeting that happened in Jabllanice on the 23rd of June that Mr. Menon has already asked you about. I'm looking at that month now. Okay?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: The document -- can you ask the question again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I haven't actually asked a question yet. What I'm saying is the questions I'm about to ask you concern that month between the meeting that the subzones were established on 23rd of May and a later meeting, a month later, in Jabllanice. Okay? I'm looking at that month now. And, first of all, we can see for ourselves that Jabllanice was not incorporated within those subzones that were established on the 23rd of May. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It was operating independently of the coordination that was agreed at that time. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, first of all, what were communications like during that month? How easy was it for the subzone commanders to communicate with each other, first of all?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: It was difficult to communicate, because the communications network and equipment did not exist, if at all -- they did not exist. And what we had, they were very -- of poor quality. And if we needed to communicate with each other or request something, we sent people in person or we met in person with each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, on the 29th of May - that's just six days after the establishment of these subzones - was there a major Serbian offensive against your village?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And was it also against other villages in your subzone, Strellc i Eperm, Boriq, Kryshec and so forth?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And did you manage to keep the Serbian forces at bay with the help of fighters from other villages?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: On the 29th of May, there was a Serbian offensive of large proportions and there were attacks in the area of Isniq and there were other directions of attacks towards Strellc i Eperm, Lugu i Baranit, Perroi i Gervalles, Rashiq, and on the same day, there were other attacks outside the subzone in Kodra e Vranocit. This was a large-scale attack and all the villages were active in organising resistance. And in the end, we were able to keep them at bay. I just wanted to add that the villages helped each other, and there was voluntary support that came to our aid from other villages. For example, Shemsedin Qeku came from Irzniq with 30 men. But because we had large numbers of people ourselves, we did not use that formation in our defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that. Generally speaking, you've talked about the -- the problems that there were in getting anything organised militarily amongst the village defences because you were engaged in fighting of Serbian offensives. Where was Ramush Haradinaj most frequently engaged during this period of May to June?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Ramush Haradinaj was mainly engaged in his own zone, and we had contact with each other. I think it was once a week. This was to analyse the situation in each zone. We thought that this was necessary to have some sort of coordination and in order to be aware of the situation in each zone during the fighting and what things we needed to change, if any.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Pausing there for a minute, again, during this period between the 23rd of May and the 23rd of June, were the five subzone commanders all of equal status?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Yes. They were of equal status.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So that Mr. Haradinaj may have had -- or the Haradinaj family may have had a special reputation for their success on the 24th of March, but they were not commanding you, were they?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: No. They were not commanding us. But we had a lot of respect for the Haradinaj family and Ramush Haradinaj, and we proposed that there should be a person who would coordinate our work and we proposed Ramush to be our coordinator. And, of course, Ramush accepted that task as he accepted other tasks which had to do with the improvement of our organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You're referring now, I think to the meeting on the 23rd of June; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: No. I'm referring to the 23rd of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: We were appointed representatives or responsible people for the five subzones and at that time we had this discussion of how we would be able to keep contact in the future. And because of our respect for him, we proposed that Ramush would be the coordinator who would coordinate the work and we would have regular meetings amongst each other. He was the person who had actually fought the Serbs, so we respected him for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And in that month we're discussing, 23rd of May to 23rd of June, although you may have had regular contacts with Mr. Haradinaj, can I put to you, it's true, isn't it, that he never once issued you an order?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Yes, that can be said. We discussed in meetings about the way how we would solve problems, and we decided jointly. So there were no orders in the sense of orders given in an advanced normal army. The notion of an order did not exist. There was consensus, and consent after we agreed on something, then the decision was taken to act upon it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, is it right that it was your idea that -- that there should be greater coordination between the subzones and the KLA base in Jabllanice? It was you who was suggesting that there should be greater communication, because Jabllanice -- partly because Jabllanice was recruiting young men without you necessarily knowing who they were or where they were coming from.

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: After we became the people responsible for the subzones, it is logical and it makes military sense that a person who is responsible militarily, or from the command point of view, should know what's going on in the area. It was not a matter of reporting, of -- or being accountable to some -- to someone. But there were requests for fighters from a certain area to go to Jabllanice. I didn't think that was very much of a concern, but professionally, I thought that it was important to ensure that every initiative, every request, because I was responsible for a certain zone, the person who was responsible for the area in question, for the zone in question should be contacted. Any kind of request, not only supporting with fire-power, but any other request. This was a time when we were teaching other people how to communicate within the military structures, and I discussed this with Ramush and I insisted to have some sort of communication so that requests coming from Jabllanice or any other place should be coordinated and we should be -- should -- aware of them and respond to them to our best ability at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. But just maybe a short answer, in very short yes-or-no form, it was your suggestion, wasn't it, that there should be this meeting on the 23rd of June to try to establish greater coordination with Jabllanice.

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, this was a suggestion from the organisational point of view. I thought it was necessary to do that because before that time there had been a request by Jabllanice village.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Again, try to keep your answers just a little bit shorter if you can. And again, no discourtesy, I'm not intending any discourtesy but we need to try to keep time moving on.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can we please look at P191 which is the minutes of that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Menon took you to a document that postdated the meeting but we actually have the minutes of the meeting itself which is P191, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we do that, Mr. Emmerson, what do you want to do with this map the witness has marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I imagine that ought to be marked as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number. That was P78, am I right?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the marked map which was taken from Exhibit P78 will now be given exhibit number D145.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. So we were looking for P191.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Whilst that document is being brought up, Mr. Rexhahmetaj, let me just ask you a couple of questions about this meeting. First of all, was it the first time you'd ever been to Jabllanice?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Yes, that was the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: In fact, was it the only time during 1998 that you ever went to Jabllanice?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: As far as I remember, yes. I think I accompanied an officer one day.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... let me stop you there. Because we don't need all the details. The point I was trying to get to with you was simply this: It's right, isn't it, that travel to Jabllanice was dangerous and difficult.

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it was like that because it was far away, and it was isolated as an area.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Pausing there, you would tend to -- people, if they had to go to Jabllanice, would have to travel at night, by and large, and with the lights on their vehicles turned off; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: I don't know what other people did when they travelled there. The night we went there, we used additional security measures during our travel there.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Did you have your headlights turned off?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: In some portions of the road, yes. I can't remember exactly. We were in the car, myself and two other people. They tended to use them on and off.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And is that because there were Serb military formations with long-range artillery stationed on high ground such as Suka e Biteshit and all of the high points, Suka e Radonjicit and so forth so that you needed to ensure that you couldn't be targeted by long-range weaponry.

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Correct. Because the lights of the car could make us -- could expose us to them and that's why we masked them.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So is it again fair to say that, generally speaking, those of you who were engaged on the western side of the zone close to the main road would only make the journey to Jabllanice when it was strictly necessary?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Given the difficulties of travel to Jabllanice, is it correct to say, I'm suggesting to you, that those of you who were commanders on -- of the four subzones, 1, 2, 3, and 4, would make that journey only if it was strictly necessary.

utterances.speaker: SKENDER REXHAHMETAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And we can see this is -- we have the full minute here in the screen in front of you of the meeting of the 23rd of June at Jabllanice. And we can see that you I think -- just to be absolutely clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Sorry, have we got the right -- I think this is the wrong minute. It's the wrong minute. Let me look at the last page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have ten minutes, please, if possible, a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: We're going to break in ten minutes is that -- inevitably, we are going to break in ten minutes, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We are, but depending on what the needs of witness maybe we should break.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: A little earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Or maybe you respond to him now.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So respond to him as in respond to his request to rise at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, well, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You want ten minutes to stand down? Would it be a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It may be a convenient time to break for the day. I don't have a great deal more for this witness but I can finish in less than half an hour tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In response to your request, Mr. Rexhahmetaj, we'll break off now. Remember, you are still on the witness-stand. You are not excused yet. You're still coming back tomorrow to come and testify. Because of that you may not discuss the case with anybody, in particular, not from anybody from the Prosecution. You are excused until tomorrow at quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon, in the same courtroom. You may stand down. And have a good rest tonight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I guess we can stop here for the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. I don't think -- unless anybody else has anything they want to raise in the last ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That would be very kind of all of you if there were nothing to raise. Thank you very much. Well, we stand adjourned to tomorrow, quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 2nd day of September, 2011, at 2.15 p.m.
